newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH PAPER UNION SAYS TO HARDLY JOIN BROAD DEAL.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH PAPER UNION SAYS TO HARDLY JOIN BROAD DEAL.

text.p: The paper workers' union is unlikely to join another nation-wide low-pay-rise incomes settlement, union chairman Jarmo Lahteenmaki was quoted as saying in a newspaper interview published on Wednesday.

He said branch unions and employer groups would be just as competent as central union and employer confederations to take into consideration key economic policy goals like low inflation and steady interest rates.
Lahteenmaki said paper workers were disappointed with the scant improvement in employment since the signing in autumn 1995 of a broad two-year pay deal with "cosmetic" wage hikes.

"We believed that such a low-level settlement would give employers the possibility to hire more people and would instil in the government the political will to create jobs, but the employment situation is unchanged," Lahteenmaki said in the interview in daily Helsingin Sanomat.
The paper workers' union was unlikely to be part of a similar broad incomes settlement.

"If it doesn't work, why set out to try again?" Lahteenmaki said. He added that he did not rule out another centralised pay deal, but only on condition that the main target would be to boost employment.
But without such a common denominator it would be "very difficult" for the paper workers' union to join a centralised incomes settlement, Lahteenmaki said.
"Since it was very difficult last time it will be even more difficult next time," he said.
The current settlement expires in February 1998 and pay talks on a deal from then onward are scheduled to begin in the autumn.
Lahteenmaki said it was fruitless to discuss the coming talks until all components of the current settlement had been implemented.

He also said the issue of whether Finland should participate in the third phase of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) should not be linked with the autumn wage talks, but rather should be discussed before summer.
"EMU matters should not be brought to the labour market negotiating table because the talks could easily turn into the kind that no one would be able to control," Lahteenmaki said.
"Decisions on the EMU (membership) terms can be made separately from the collective bargaining round -- and before it," he said.
